subject: History
chapter: Peasants, Zamindars and the State: Agrarian Society and the Mughal Empire
central_question: How were production, community, power and revenue organised in Mughal rural society, and how can the Ain-i Akbari and regional records be used to reconstruct them?
in_scope_units: Sources for Mughal agrarian history and the viewpoint of the Ain-i Akbari.
Peasant categories, mobility, landholding and village production.
Irrigation, tools, crops and commercial agriculture.
Caste, panchayats, headmen, artisans and women in the village community.
Forest dwellers, shifting cultivation and agrarian expansion.
Zamindar rights, revenue collection and local authority.
Monetary transactions, markets, credit and the flow of silver.
Organisation, statistical content and limitations of the Ain-i Akbari.
banned_topics: Permanent Settlement and colonial revenue auctions, treated in the next chapter.
A general political narrative of Mughal emperors beyond agrarian administration.

known_pitfalls.claim: The Ain gives a neutral peasant account of rural society.
known_pitfalls.correction: It is a courtly administrative text presenting an imperial view and must be compared with regional records and evidence of conflict.

known_pitfalls.claim: Mughal agriculture was only subsistence farming.
known_pitfalls.correction: Staples were combined with cash crops, multiple cropping, markets and monetary revenue demands.

known_pitfalls.claim: A zamindar privately owned all village land in the modern sense.
known_pitfalls.correction: Zamindars held superior fiscal and social rights, while peasants also possessed and transferred their fields.
